competition_series: FSG (Formula Student Germany), FS Czech, FS East
summary: Chalmers Formula Student added a driverless program (CFSD) onto an already-running electric car platform (EV since 2015), starting development in autumn 2017 with 15 students (7 returning from the EV team, 8 new) and debuting at FSG 2018 roughly 10-11 months later. The program grew from a custom OpenDLV/C++ microservice stack (CFSD18/CFSD19) into a mature, largely in-house (~97% self-built) autonomous system that won the FSG Driverless Cup outright in 2023 and 2025 (car 'Svea'). The team publishes numerous Chalmers master's theses each year covering hardware (steering actuation, sensor packaging, aero) and software (perception, planning) subsystems, making it one of the best-documented veteran DV programs. Team scale is now roughly 60 students total working ~6 months near-full-time per season, with a small dedicated DV hardware/software cohort. Their build-on-existing-EV-platform approach and ~10-month first-competition timeline is highly analogous to UMSAE's situation.

ramp_phases: [uncertain] Not explicitly named by the team in sources reviewed; inferred phases are (1) thesis-project conception (autumn 2017), (2) first debut build reusing 2017 EV chassis (2018), (3) iterative CFSD18/CFSD19 in-house microservice refinement (2018-2019), (4) mature, largely self-built competitive program (2022-2026)
what_slipped: [uncertain] No explicit team statement of schedule slips found in public sources. Indirect evidence: no FSG Driverless result was found for 2020-2021 (likely COVID-19 disruption to the wider FSG calendar, consistent with cancellations across the series), and results dip sharply between strong years (e.g., 1st in 2023 to 2nd/3rd in 2024, and back to 7th in 2026), suggesting year-over-year performance volatility tied to new-team knowledge transfer rather than a single named slip.
platform_prerequisites: Yes - driverless was built onto an existing, already-running Formula Student Electric platform (Chalmers transitioned to EV in 2015; CFSD18 reused the 2017 electric car's carbon-fiber monocoque chassis). No separate EV-conversion phase was needed before DV work began, directly analogous to UMSAE's existing-EV starting position.
ebs_design: [uncertain] Specific EBS architecture (pneumatic vs. hydraulic accumulator, actuator model) not found in sources reviewed for Chalmers specifically; team's public GitHub/thesis material found covers steering and perception rather than EBS. General FSAE DT.3.2 requirement (passive mechanically-stored-energy system, <=200ms reaction time per DT.3.2.5.a, >10 m/s^2 average deceleration per DT.3.2.5.b, half performance on single failure per DT.3.2.5.c) applies but no Chalmers-specific implementation detail was sourced.
steering_actuation: Rack-parallel ball-screw actuator driven by a brushless servo motor, coupled to the steering rack via a cross bore and shoulder screw, mounted directly on/at the steering rack. Steers full-left to full-right in 0.4 seconds and provides 2000 N at the rack with the car stationary (matches manual-driver performance ~99% of the time per prior Autocross telemetry). The ball screw's low friction and lack of self-retention allows the driver to steer manually when the actuator is decoupled, satisfying DT.2.2 actuator decoupling and manual-mode retention. Assembly is removable via 8 bolts plus the shoulder screw for quick servicing.
brake_actuation: [uncertain] Not detailed in sources reviewed beyond general references to the car's hydraulic service brakes
sensor_mounting_packaging: [uncertain] General thesis title references an aerodynamic package, steering actuation, and computer case as the three subsystems covered by a single hardware-development thesis, implying sensor/compute packaging was a first-order design constraint, but specific envelope/DT.2.3 compliance detail was not retrievable (source page returned server errors on direct fetch; only search-index summaries available).
chassis_impact: Minimal - CFSD18 reused the existing 2017 EV carbon-fiber monocoque/aluminum-honeycomb chassis (2,891mm L x 1,465mm W) rather than requiring a new chassis; changes were additive (sensor mounts, compute case, actuator mounting) rather than structural redesign, per the hardware-development thesis scope.
compute_platform: 2018: custom AMD Ryzen-based compute box (OpenDLV/Docker microservices). Later years (per team engineering statements): tightly CPU-constrained onboard compute running LiDAR point-cloud processing with a documented fail-safe ('if we lose a point cloud, the car will hit the brakes'). Specific current-generation compute model (e.g., Jetson) not confirmed in sources reviewed.
sensor_suite: 2018 (CFSD18): Velodyne Puck LiDAR (primary), Stereolabs ZED stereo camera, SBG Systems Ellipse-N miniature INS with embedded GNSS (RTK mode: ~1cm position accuracy, 0.2 deg heading accuracy under high dynamics, 47g unit weight). Later years: LiDAR remains primary perception sensor with cameras for fusion; team has since published 'coneScenes,' a LiDAR dataset with 3D-annotated cones for FS driverless perception training. Cone-detection thesis reported [uncertain] ~12m detection range at 25Hz using a computer-vision approach.
shutdown_circuit_implementation: [uncertain] Not detailed in sources reviewed; general FSAE DT.4 requirements apply (Driverless System Relay DT.4.1, Remote Stop Relay DT.4.2, Emergency Brake System Relay DT.4.3) but no Chalmers-specific wiring/integration detail sourced.
remote_stop_system: [uncertain] Not detailed in sources reviewed beyond the general FSG-mandated Remote Stop System (Vehicle Module, Control Box, Remote Stop Relay)
custom_pcbs: [uncertain] Not found in sources reviewed; team's public repos include an STM32 service node described as 'replacement for BeagleBone to handle readings from car's non-driverless sensors,' implying at least some custom embedded hardware, but no PCB design/fab/bring-up duration was sourced.
software_stack: C++ throughout; originally built on the team's own OpenDLV framework as a microservices architecture running in Docker containers (CFSD18/CFSD19 generation, repo names like cfsd-microservice-template, cfsd-proxy-cangw-lynx). Later transitioned to ROS 2 for CAN data broadcast and system integration, with Foxglove, SocketCAN, and SavvyCAN used for debugging/analysis. Four separate CAN buses (steering, actuators, main vehicle network) plus Ethernet for LiDAR and telemetry; 100 Hz control loop.
ros_version: None initially (custom OpenDLV microservice middleware for CFSD18/19); ROS 2 in more recent seasons (exact distribution, e.g. Humble/Foxy, not confirmed in sources reviewed) [uncertain: exact ROS2 distro]
perception_approach: 2018: LiDAR-first fusion approach - cone positions from the Velodyne Puck LiDAR used to define Regions of Interest (ROIs) that are then classified by a CNN using the Stereolabs ZED camera. A dedicated cone-detection thesis reports [uncertain] a computer-vision approach reaching approximately 12m range at 25Hz. Team has since built and open-sourced 'coneScenes,' a LiDAR point-cloud dataset with 3D-annotated cone bounding boxes for training perception models, indicating a continued LiDAR-centric perception strategy.
slam_localization_approach: [uncertain] Public repo 'opendlv-logic-sensation-slam-cfsd' confirms a dedicated SLAM module existed from the CFSD generation, but the specific algorithm (EKF/GraphSLAM/FastSLAM) was not retrievable from sources reviewed. SBG Ellipse-N GNSS/INS (RTK, ~1cm position accuracy) provides a strong absolute-position input alongside SLAM.
planning_approach: CFSD19 path planner (public repo cfsd-logic-pathplanner) outputs the middle path between detected cone lines (midline planning approach), with a separate longitudinal-control module (cfsd-action-longitudinal-control) for speed. A 2026 paper on adaptive velocity planning describing continuous stability-aware speed profiling and ~35% lap-time improvement over 10 laps may be affiliated with the team [uncertain - exact affiliation not confirmed in sources reviewed].
control_approach: [uncertain] Specific lateral controller (pure pursuit/Stanley/MPC) not confirmed in sources reviewed; public repo 'cfsd19-logic-lynx-steering' and 'cfsd-logic-lynx-mission-control' indicate a dedicated steering-control and mission-control module ('Lynx') existed from CFSD19 onward.
simulation_tooling: [uncertain] No specific simulator (eufs_sim/FSDS/Gazebo/CARLA/custom) confirmed for Chalmers in sources reviewed; one archived repo name ('opendlv-sim-cfsd18-cognition-blackbox') suggests an early custom OpenDLV-based simulation/cognition testbed for CFSD18.
data_logging: Foxglove used for visualization/analysis; SocketCAN and SavvyCAN used for CAN bus logging, load optimization, and debugging (per Kvaser case study).
open_source_repos: https://github.com/chalmersfsd (organization with 59 total repositories covering the CFSD18/CFSD19 generation: perception, path planning, SLAM, steering control, mission control, CAN gateway, and microservice templates - useful as a historical reference for OpenDLV-based FS driverless architecture, though largely archived/legacy); https://github.com/Chalmers-Formula-Student/coneScenes (LiDAR cone-annotation dataset for perception training, described by the team as currently inactive for public distribution beyond a sample scene).
critical_path_items: 1) Sensor/compute procurement and integration (LiDAR, GNSS/INS, compute box) onto an existing chassis within a single season; 2) steering actuator design able to satisfy both actuation performance (0.4s lock-to-lock) and DT.2.2 manual-mode decoupling without adding excessive complexity (team noted the resulting design had drawbacks - play and complexity - but was kept because it was robust); 3) building a full software stack (perception, SLAM, planning, control) from scratch in the OpenDLV framework by a first-year, largely new 15-person team.

rules_compliance_challenges: [uncertain] No explicit team statement of which rules were hardest found in sources reviewed. Inferred from design choices: satisfying DT.2.2 actuator decoupling (no parts removed, does not block manual operation in any position) while keeping the steering actuator simple appears to have been a real design tension, since the team explicitly kept a design they described as having 'play and complexity' because it was 'robust' rather than iterating to a cleaner solution.
documentation_burden: High - team consistently produces multiple Chalmers master's theses per year on DV subsystems (steering/aero/compute-case hardware, cone-detection perception) as part of students' formal thesis requirements, in addition to standard FSG driverless documentation (DSF, design reports, status videos). This academic-thesis requirement effectively doubles as their internal documentation burden and is a notable structural difference from teams without a formal thesis-credit pipeline.

team_structure_dv: 2018 (debut year): 15 second-year master's students total (7 carried over from the prior year's electric team + 8 new members), organized into three groups: (1) perception and interpretation of surroundings, (2) driving planning and control, (3) mechanical and electronic hardware for control-signal execution. Later years: overall team scale grown to roughly 60 students across mechanical, embedded systems, software engineering, and autonomous-systems specializations, with roughly six months of near-full-time work per season; some members receive academic credit via master's thesis programs, which structurally ties DV subteam membership to the university's thesis pipeline.
recruiting_and_knowledge_transfer: Structural mechanism: DV team composition is explicitly refreshed every year with new members alongside a smaller returning cohort (7 of 15 returning in the 2018 debut year is the only concrete ratio found), and a portion of the team is recruited via the university's formal master's thesis assignment process rather than pure club recruiting - this ties turnover to the academic calendar and gives incoming members built-in mentorship/thesis-supervision structure, but the team is not documented as having solved a steep learning curve; search summaries note the team 'depend[s] on the knowledge from previous years and experience a steep learning curve during the project life cycle' each season. [uncertain: source page for this specific characterization could not be independently verified via direct fetch.]
budget_estimate: [uncertain] No total or per-year USD/SEK budget figure found in sources reviewed. Known sponsors relevant to the DV program include AFRY (sponsoring the team's driverless compute hardware since 2018), ESSIQ AB, Volvo Cars, Aros Electronics AB, and WirelessCar (sponsorship extended 2024), plus Chalmers University itself; no dollar figures were disclosed publicly.
recommended_sequence: Synthesized from Chalmers' history (not an explicit team statement): 1) Start from an existing, proven EV chassis/platform rather than building a new car - do not let chassis development compete with DV integration for the first cycle. 2) Recruit a small (~15-person), cross-disciplinary founding cohort split into perception, planning/control, and mechanical/electronics sub-groups from day one. 3) Select a small, well-supported core sensor set first (one LiDAR, one camera, one INS/GNSS with RTK) rather than a large sensor suite, and get end-to-end perception-to-actuation working before adding sensors. 4) Build steering actuation and its manual-mode decoupling early and keep it simple/robust even if imperfect, since it directly gates DT.2.2 tech inspection. 5) Enter the first driverless competition on the very first eligible car (do not wait for a 'perfect' first entry) - Chalmers' 11th-place 2018 debut, ~10-11 months after program start, still scored and established the program's competition cadence.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: Highly applicable. Chalmers demonstrates that a team starting driverless work on top of an already-running EV platform (UMSAE's exact situation) can reach a first scored competition entry in roughly 10-11 months with a first-year DV cohort of only ~15 students, well within a 24-month window. UMSAE (9 software-focused members) is smaller than Chalmers' founding cohort, so UMSAE should expect either a longer timeline to first competition or a deliberately narrower initial scope (e.g., fewer sensors, simpler planner) to compensate for headcount. The Chalmers pattern of splitting the team into three groups (perception, planning/control, mechanical-electrical) from day one is directly reusable. UMSAE should also copy Chalmers' 'keep the steering actuator simple and robust rather than iterating for polish' discipline, and its practice of using LiDAR as the primary/first perception sensor with camera fusion added afterward rather than a camera-first approach. One risk to avoid: Chalmers shows a documented steep year-over-year learning curve from turnover even with an ~50% returning-member ratio in its debut year - UMSAE, with a fixed small team, should invest early in written internal documentation (not just theses/reports for FSG) to reduce this risk, since Chalmers' primary knowledge-transfer mechanism (the university thesis pipeline) is not available to UMSAE in the same form.
